title: 2 Chronicles 4:1–10
context: The Chronicler continues the furnishing of the house begun in chapter 3, moving from the bronze works in the court to the gold furnishings inside: the bronze altar (4:1), the molten sea on twelve oxen (4:2–5), ten basins (4:6), ten gold lamp stands (4:7), ten tables and one hundred gold basins (4:8), the courts (4:9), and the placing of the sea (4:10). The parallel is 1 Kings 7:23–39, with the lamp stands and table at 1 Kings 7:48–49. Differences are named rather than harmonized: 1 Kings 7 gives no dimensions for a bronze altar, though 1 Kings 8:64 mentions the bronze altar; 2 Chronicles 4:3 describes the likeness of oxen under the sea, where 1 Kings 7:24 describes buds; 2 Chronicles 4:5 says the sea received and held three thousand baths, where 1 Kings 7:26 says it held two thousand; and 2 Chronicles 4:8 says Solomon made ten tables, where 1 Kings 7:48 names the table in the singular. As at 1 Kings 7:23–39, 2 Chronicles 4:6 states that the basins were for washing the offerings and the sea for the priests, in continuity with the bronze basin of the tabernacle (Exodus 30:18–21). The Chronicler has already presented the work as following the pattern David received (1 Chronicles 28:11–19). Arminian and Reformed readers alike treat this unit as description of provision for worship, and neither tradition draws a doctrinal disagreement from the furnishings.

verses.text: Then he made an altar of bronze, twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and ten cubits high.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon makes a great bronze altar, twenty cubits long and wide and ten high, far larger than the tabernacle altar of Exodus 27:1. Arminian readers see the scale as fitting for a settled nation gathered at one place of sacrifice, where the people could come near to God through the offerings he had appointed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the altar as the center of the sacrificial worship God appointed, now enlarged for the permanent house. Shared ground: both traditions see the altar as a reminder that sinful people approach a holy God only on the terms he provides, and both read the dimensions as plain description rather than code.

verses.text: Also he made the molten sea of ten cubits from brim to brim. It was round, five cubits high, and thirty cubits in circumference.
verses.arminianNotes: The molten sea is ten cubits across, five high, and thirty around, matching the measurements in 1 Kings 7:23. Arminian readers note the size and skill of the casting and read the figures as practical description, offered so that later readers could picture the great basin that stood in the court.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly treat the dimensions as historical description of a real vessel made for the LORD’s service, consistent with the approach taken at 1 Kings 7:23. Shared ground: both traditions decline to build doctrine on the relation of the figures and read the verse as honoring careful, costly work.

verses.text: Under it was the likeness of oxen, which encircled it, for ten cubits, encircling the sea. The oxen were in two rows, cast when it was cast.
verses.arminianNotes: Under the sea the Chronicler describes the likeness of oxen in two rows, cast with the sea, where 1 Kings 7:24 describes buds. Arminian readers note the difference plainly and do not resolve it by speculation; they read the verse as part of a faithful record of craftsmanship devoted to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise name the parallel difference honestly and affirm that Scripture’s trustworthiness does not depend on forcing every detail of parallel accounts into agreement. Shared ground: both traditions treat the ornament as decoration of the sea and see no theological question turning on it.

verses.text: It stood on twelve oxen, three looking toward the north, three looking toward the west, three looking toward the south, and three looking toward the east; and the sea was set on them above, and all their hindquarters were inward.
verses.arminianNotes: The sea stands on twelve oxen, three facing each direction, with their hindquarters inward, as in 1 Kings 7:25. Arminian readers note the symmetry of the design. Many readers associate the number twelve with Israel’s tribes, but the text itself does not say so, and Arminian readers hold that suggestion loosely.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also recognize that some interpreters link the twelve oxen with the twelve tribes, while noting that the Chronicler draws no such connection. Shared ground: both traditions read the oxen as part of a magnificent, ordered design for worship and avoid resting any doctrine on a symbolism the text does not state.

verses.text: It was a handbreadth thick. Its brim was made like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily. It received and held three thousand baths.
verses.arminianNotes: The sea is a handbreadth thick, its brim shaped like a lily, and it received and held three thousand baths, where 1 Kings 7:26 gives two thousand. Arminian readers state the difference as it stands without harmonizing it, and they read the verse as emphasizing the great capacity of the vessel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the different figure in 1 Kings 7:26 without proposing a forced reconciliation. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing the elegance and scale of the sea, and both hold that the trustworthiness of the record is not threatened by naming such differences honestly.

verses.text: He also made ten basins, and put five on the right hand and five on the left, to wash in them. The things that belonged to the burnt offering were washed in them, but the sea was for the priests to wash in.
verses.arminianNotes: The ten basins are for washing the things that belonged to the burnt offering, while the sea is for the priests to wash in. Arminian readers see the concern for cleansing as continuous with the bronze basin of Exodus 30:18–21 and as a reminder that those who serve before God must come prepared and clean.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly connect the washing with the tabernacle basin and see in it God’s provision for priests who are not clean in themselves. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as explaining the purpose of the bronze vessels, which 1 Kings 7:38–39 describes without stating their use.

verses.text: He made the ten lamp stands of gold according to the ordinance concerning them; and he set them in the temple, five on the right hand and five on the left.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon makes ten gold lamp stands according to the ordinance concerning them and sets five on each side, as 1 Kings 7:49 also says. Arminian readers note the phrase “according to the ordinance” and see worship that follows what God has given rather than human invention, even as it expands to suit the new house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress that the lamp stands are made according to God’s ordinance, in keeping with the pattern given to David (1 Chronicles 28:11–19). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the temple’s worship stands in continuity with the tabernacle’s and is ordered by God’s word.

verses.text: He made also ten tables, and placed them in the temple, five on the right side and five on the left. He made one hundred basins of gold.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon makes ten tables, five on each side, and one hundred gold basins, where 1 Kings 7:48 names the table for the show bread in the singular. Arminian readers note the difference without resolving it and see the verse as describing abundant provision for the daily service of the house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also state the parallel difference plainly and decline to harmonize it by speculation. Shared ground: both traditions read the multiplied tables and basins as signs of the generous, ordered provision made for the LORD’s house, and neither tradition draws a doctrinal point from the number.

verses.text: Furthermore he made the court of the priests, the great court, and doors for the court, and overlaid their doors with bronze.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon makes the court of the priests and the great court, with bronze-overlaid doors. Arminian readers see an ordered approach to God in the distinction between the courts: the house is open to the gathered people for worship, while different spaces are set apart for different kinds of service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the courts as expressing God’s holiness and the order he gives to worship, with the priests’ court set apart for their ministry. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as construction description and avoid assigning precise meanings to the courts beyond what the text states.

verses.text: He set the sea on the right side of the house eastward, toward the south.
verses.arminianNotes: The sea is set on the right side of the house, eastward and toward the south, as in 1 Kings 7:39. Arminian readers read the note as practical detail that locates the great basin within the court, completing the description of where the priests would wash before their service at the altar.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the placement as historical detail that anchors the account in a real building. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as closing this list of furnishings, and both see the care given to arrangement as fitting for a house built for the name of the LORD.
